chunks.text: 3 Materials and Methods 3.1 Datasets BACH [ 8 ] : 400 H&E images, 4 balanced classes (accuracy reported), native resolution (0.42 μ \mu m/pixel), SLIC target of 800 superpixels per image (625 on average); 5-fold stratified cross-validation repeated 3 times (15 folds), identical across encoders. BRACS [ 9 ] : 7-class breast lesion subtyping on the official train/val/test split. RoIs are scanned at 0.25 μ \mu m/pixel and vary in size, so each image is center-cropped to 1000 × 1000 1000{\times}1000 px (smaller images, 31%, are excluded, leaving 2,584/221/321 of the official 3,657/312/570 train/val/test images) and segmented with a target of 250 superpixels (197 on average), matching BACH’s superpixel size in pixels (median 4,645 vs. 4,617) but not in tissue area, which is about a third (290 vs. 810 μ \mu m 2 ). With a fixed split, TAN, TAN-unmasked, ResNet18-scratch and each GAT are trained with 5 seeds and reported as mean ± \pm std over seeds. After the filter, the training split holds 213 (UDH) to 591 (PB) images per class and the test split 25 (FEA) to 64 (IC), so macro-F1 is reported alongside accuracy; the filter is class-skewed, keeping 90% of IC but only 38% of FEA, 55% of UDH and 59% of ADH images. 3.2 Superpixel Graph Construction Images are segmented with SLIC [ 14 ] ; the superpixels, without further merging, are the nodes of the tissue graph, and two nodes are connected by an undirected edge if their regions share a pixel border. Every encoder sees only its own superpixel’s masked content, so node embeddings are context-free: neighborhood information enters only through the graph classifier. For encoders with standard convolution, pixels outside the mask are replaced by the superpixel’s mean color ( mean fill ) or by constant white ( white fill ); results are reported for both. TAN receives the raw crop plus the mask and needs no fill value.

3.3 TAN: Tissue-Aware Network Figure 1: TAN encoder: four stages of masked convolution (SolidConv), mask-aware GroupNorm, LeakyReLU, and masked 2 × 2 2{\times}2 max-pooling (32, 64, 128, 128 channels), then masked attention pooling to a 1024-d node embedding. The mask is downsampled alongside the features; invalid positions are ignored in every operation. TAN is a 4-stage encoder (Fig. 1 ). Each stage applies a masked convolution ( SolidConv : a pixel’s output is computed only if its full 3 × 3 3\times 3 neighborhood lies within the current mask), mask-aware GroupNorm (statistics over valid positions), LeakyReLU, and masked 2 × 2 2\times 2 max-pooling (invalid positions cannot win), with 32, 64, 128 and 128 channels. An 8-head attention pooling, whose softmax excludes invalid positions, yields a 1024-d embedding that feeds a linear classifier head. TAN passes the superpixel mask on unchanged, only downsampling it by pooling between stages, so the valid region keeps the superpixel’s shape (up to pooling resolution), and a position receives a data-dependent output only if its entire 3 × 3 3\times 3 neighborhood lies within the mask, so boundary outputs never mix in implicit zeros. The outermost ring of valid positions at each stage therefore carries only the layer’s normalized bias term and no local image content (light gray in Fig. 2 ). Superpixels without any fully valid 3 × 3 3\times 3 neighborhood at some stage carry no image content: 0.001% (3 of 249,800) on BACH, 0.003% (16 of 616,769) on BRACS. Crops of similar area are batched and zero-padded to the batch maximum; the padded values lie outside the mask and cannot contaminate any operation (embeddings are identical to float precision when the padding preserves the pooling alignment). TAN is not pretrained externally: each superpixel is trained to predict its image’s class, a weak, noisy but dense signal.

On BACH, TAN is retrained for every cross-validation fold (15% of the fold’s training images held out for early stopping); on BRACS it is trained on the filtered official training split (2,584 images) with the filtered official validation split (221 images) for early stopping, once per seed. TAN, TAN-unmasked and ResNet18-scratch share the augmentation function (flips, 90-degree rotations, intensity jitter) and the epoch limit, patience, learning rate and weight decay; batch sizes differ (Section 3.4 ). Figure 2: A superpixel from a BRACS test image passing through a trained TAN. Top row: input crop with the superpixel outline and, for stages 1–4, the channel mean of each stage’s output. Bottom row: the mask and the strongest channel of each stage, i.e., the channel with the largest spatial variance. Dark gray: outside the mask; light gray: inside the mask but without a fully valid 3 × 3 3{\times}3 neighborhood (bias only). Panels are scaled independently. 3.4 Comparison Encoders TAN-unmasked isolates masked processing: it has TAN’s architecture, parameters (408,580), augmentation, size-sorted batching and training settings (batch size 16), but the pixels outside the mask are replaced by the fill (batches are padded with each crop’s own fill color) and processed like any other pixel by standard convolution, GroupNorm, max-pooling and attention over all positions; it is evaluated on both datasets. ResNet18-scratch is a standard randomly initialized ResNet18 [ 15 ] (11,178,564 parameters) trained with the same protocol as TAN (same superpixel-level image-label supervision, per-fold retraining, epochs, patience, learning rate and weight decay; batch size 32 vs. 16) on a masked 128 × 128 128\times 128 crop: an architecture control, evaluated on both datasets. ResNet18-ImageNet , CTransPath [ 11 ] and UNI [ 10 ] are frozen encoders pretrained on ImageNet, TCGA+PAIP, and a large, mostly private histopathology corpus.

Masked crops are extracted at each encoder’s input resolution ( 128 × 128 128\times 128 ; 224 × 224 224\times 224 for CTransPath and UNI), never resized, and normalized with ImageNet channel statistics. 3.5 Downstream Classifier and Protocol A 3-layer GAT [ 16 ] (4 attention heads per layer) with mean/max pooling classifies each graph from its node embeddings. As is usual for UNI and CTransPath, the frozen backbones (like ResNet18-ImageNet) are not adapted; only the GAT is trained on their embeddings. A Random Forest on pooled (mean/std/min/max/median) per-image statistics of the node features is a non-graph reference. 3.6 Statistical Methodology On BACH, folds of repeated cross-validation share training data and, across repeats, test data, so naive paired tests understate the variance [ 17 , 18 ] . We use the Nadeau–Bengio corrected resampled t t -test [ 18 ] , applied to repeated k k -fold cross-validation as in [ 19 ] , which scales the variance by ( 1 / J + n test / n train ) (1/J+n_{\text{test}}/n_{\text{train}}) with J = 15 J=15 the total number of train/test splits (5 folds × \times 3 repeats), with Holm–Bonferroni correction over the five comparisons against TAN (per fill condition), and call differences significant at corrected p < 0.05 p<0.05 . TAN is numerically first under mean fill and second to UNI under white fill, and is not significantly different from UNI or from TAN-unmasked in either case (corrected p = 1.0 p=1.0 ). It is 4.3 pp above ResNet18-scratch under mean fill (better in 12 of 15 folds), but not significantly after correction ( p = 0.49 p=0.49 ; 0.72 0.72 under white fill), and a non-significant difference does not establish equivalence: with 15 folds the test has limited power. Under mean fill TAN is 9.9 pp above CTransPath (14 of 15 folds), which does not survive correction ( p = 0.065 p=0.065 ; uncorrected 0.016 0.016 ), and clearly above ResNet18-ImageNet ( p = 0.001 p=0.001 ); under white fill neither is significant ( p = 0.62 p=0.62 , 0.08 0.08 ). The ablation isolates masked processing: TAN-unmasked matches TAN under mean fill ( 80.9 80.9 vs. 81.1 81.1 ; TAN better in 9 of 15 folds) and is 1.8 pp lower under white fill ( 79.3 79.3 ; corrected p = 1.0 p=1.0 , uncorrected 0.61 0.61 ). Masking thus does not improve accuracy on BACH. Its measurable effects are compute (0.10 vs. 0.22 GFLOPs per superpixel, ≈ 2.2 × {\approx}2.2\times ) and fill dependence: TAN-unmasked changes by 1.6 pp between the two fills, whereas a trained TAN’s embeddings were bit-identical under four backgrounds (original, white, mean, random noise) on 100 random BRACS superpixels, while a frozen ResNet18’s differed by a median of 64% of their norm between white and mean fill.

TAN has ≈ 27 × {\approx}27\times and ≈ 740 × {\approx}740\times fewer parameters than ResNet18-scratch and UNI and needs on average 0.10 GFLOPs per superpixel (std 0.05), ≈ \approx 1,190 × \times fewer than UNI and ≈ 11.8 × {\approx}11.8\times fewer than ResNet18 at 128 × 128 128\times 128 , which process a full window per superpixel, mostly fill. The background fill changes the frozen encoders by up to 6 pp (white fill: ResNet18-ImageNet + 6.1 +6.1 , CTransPath + 4.4 +4.4 , UNI + 1.9 +1.9 ), more than the differences among the four best encoders under mean fill (at most 4.3 pp); the from-scratch networks change less ( − 1.2 -1.2 ResNet18-scratch, − 1.6 -1.6 TAN-unmasked; within fold-level std). 4.2 Results on BRACS Table 2: BRACS, official split, 5 seeds (mean ± \pm population std over seeds, %). Superpixels have no labels of their own (TAN is trained with the class of its image, a multiple-instance setting), and the tissue structures they contain are not annotated; together with context-free embeddings, this weak supervision may explain the low absolute accuracies, which are not comparable to image-level results (all experiments use RoIs, not complete WSIs). Generality.

BRACS has one split and a class-skewed filter, and TAN’s embeddings depend on batch padding through floor pooling (padding to multiples of 16 should remove this). The superpixel size was matched in pixels, not in tissue area (Section 3.1 ), and was not tuned; this difference in scale could contribute to the different results of TAN relative to the foundation models on the two datasets, and further experiments with other datasets and resolutions and a study of the superpixel size are needed to evaluate this and to find the best superpixel size. 6 Conclusion We introduced TAN, a 0.41M-parameter encoder that keeps tissue regions intact and excludes background from every operation, so its embeddings are exactly invariant to the fill, which matters in medical imaging. On BACH its accuracy is not significantly different from the 303M-parameter UNI, with ≈ 740 × {\approx}740\times fewer parameters, ≈ 1,190 × {\approx}1{,}190\times fewer FLOPs and no pretraining; on BRACS it is close to ResNet18 but behind UNI and CTransPath. An unmasked twin reaches similar accuracy (nominally lower on BACH, higher on BRACS) at more than twice the FLOPs. Whether pretraining or a better superpixel size closes the BRACS gap remains open.
